case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes the President to impose tariffs as an emergency economic measure.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (IEEPA) (and, in the consolidated government petition, the related constitutional question whether IEEPA would be an unconstitutional delegation if it does authorize tariffs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (e.g., Learning Resources) argue that IEEPA does not grant the President authority to impose tariffs because tariffs are a distinct, congressionally controlled tool of raising revenue/regulating trade and are not among the specific transaction-blocking powers Congress enumerated in § 1702(a)(1)(B). They contend that reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would improperly convert a targeted emergency power (blocking/prohibiting certain dealings in property) into a broad trade-and-tax authority that Congress has historically conferred only through more specific tariff statutes. Petitioners also press that resolving the statutory meaning is a purely legal question suitable for immediate Supreme Court review to provide certainty, and they resist jurisdictional/venue maneuvers designed to delay merits resolution (e.g., transferring to the Court of International Trade).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents/government argue that IEEPA’s broad emergency powers over economic transactions with a foreign nexus are sufficient to encompass tariff-like exactions as a means of regulating or restricting foreign commerce during a declared national emergency. They additionally argue that challenges to the President’s compliance with emergency predicates (e.g., whether an 'unusual and extraordinary threat' exists or whether the President’s findings are adequate) are nonjusticiable political questions committed to Congress under the statutory scheme for reviewing emergencies. In the consolidated posture reflected in the filings, the government also frames a fallback: if IEEPA is construed to authorize tariffs, the Court must address whether that construction creates an unconstitutional delegation of legislative/taxing authority.
key_precedents: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc. (referenced for Court of International Trade jurisdiction/§ 1581(i) channeling)
BP p.l.c. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (referenced for the weakness of congressional 'ratification' arguments in statutory interpretation absent settled, uniform precedent)
Tett (D.D.C. decision referenced in argument transcript for political question/nonreviewability themes)
International Labor (D.D.C. case referenced for the 'arises under' analysis tied to the substantive legal theory)

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s strongest argument is textual: §1702(a)(1)(B) uses broad verbs—“regulate” and “prohibit”—and it expressly mentions “importation,” so a tariff can be characterized as a form of import regulation during an emergency. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress, those verbs operate on a defined object—“transactions” involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest”—and a generally applicable duty assessed on domestic importers at entry does not fit that transaction/property-with-foreign-interest architecture. Given Congress’s longstanding, detailed tariff and trade statutes, I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that we should not infer that IEEPA silently displaces that framework for a decision of this magnitude absent a clear statement. We can therefore resolve on statutory grounds (placing the action at least outside clear congressional authorization in Youngstown terms) and avoid reaching nondelegation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s strongest argument is that §1702(a)(1)(B) expressly mentions “importation” and uses broad verbs like “regulate,” which—at a high level—could be said to include a tariff as one mode of regulating imports. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, those verbs operate on a limiting object: “transactions involving … property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” language that naturally targets blocking and transactional controls, not a generally applicable duty assessed on domestic importers at the border. And as the Chief Justice notes, Congress has enacted detailed tariff and revenue schemes; it is implausible to treat IEEPA as silently reallocating that quintessentially congressional foreign-commerce and taxing leverage to the Executive without a clear statement. Because the statute itself supplies a workable limit, we should resolve the case on statutory grounds and avoid unnecessary constitutional adjudication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that §1702(a)(1)(B) uses capacious verbs—“regulate” and “prohibit”—and mentions “importation,” so a tariff might be cast as just another form of import regulation in an emergency. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, those verbs operate on a limiting object: “transactions” involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” a structure that fits blocking and transactional controls far more naturally than an across-the-board duty assessed on domestic importers at entry. Justice Thomas’s structural concern is decisive for me: reading IEEPA to authorize tariffs would silently displace Congress’s detailed trade-and-tariff statutes and their procedural choices, effectively making that framework optional whenever the Executive invokes an emergency. On that statutory reading, we can resolve the case without reaching nondelegation or other constitutional questions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s best contention is that IEEPA’s broad verbs—particularly “regulate” and “prohibit,” coupled with the reference to “importation”—can encompass tariff-like measures as emergency tools. But, as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, those verbs operate on a defined object: “transactions” involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” a foreign-property nexus that fits blocking and transactional controls, not a generally applicable duty imposed on domestic importers at entry. Given Congress’s long practice of addressing tariffs through tariff-specific statutes, I agree with Justice Barrett that we should not read IEEPA to silently displace that framework without a clear textual statement. Resolving on statutory grounds also preserves judicial review against emergency rhetoric and avoids unnecessary constitutional delegation disputes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that IEEPA is built for speed and flexibility in emergencies, and §1702’s verbs (“regulate,” “prohibit”) are undeniably broad—broad enough to reach many import-related measures. But as Justice Barrett persuasively frames it, those verbs are tethered to a particular object: “transactions” involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” a transactional/property architecture that naturally fits blocking and transfer controls, not a generally applicable tariff that operates as an import duty assessed on domestic importers at entry. The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh reinforce that reading by situating IEEPA alongside Congress’s detailed tariff statutes; absent clearer textual connection, we should not treat IEEPA as silently converting an emergency sanctions tool into a general tariff statute. Because that limit comes from the statute’s own nouns and structure—not from scale-based skepticism—I remain with petitioner and would resolve on statutory grounds without reaching nondelegation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains that §1702(a)(1)(B) uses capacious verbs—especially “regulate” and “prohibit”—and expressly reaches “importation,” so a tariff might be characterized as just another import regulation. But as Justice Kagan stresses, even broad verbs take their meaning from their objects: here, “transactions involving… property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” which fits blocking or conditioning discrete dealings, not rewriting the tariff schedule through a generally applicable border exaction. Justice Barrett’s observation about the mismatch between IEEPA’s property/transaction architecture and tariffs’ revenue-and-trade operation underscores the anti-surplusage problem: the foreign-property nexus would do little limiting work under the Government’s reading. And as the Chief Justice notes, accepting this atextual expansion would effectively displace Congress’s detailed tariff delegations without any clear textual instruction—something separation-of-powers principles counsel us to resist and our duty is to enforce, not revise.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is that IEEPA is a foreign-affairs/national-security statute and that §1702(a)(1)(B)’s broad verbs (“regulate,” “prohibit”) plus the reference to “importation” could be read to include a tariff-like measure. But, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, those verbs operate on a defined object—“transactions involving … property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest”—which fits asset-blocking and transactional controls, not a generally applicable border duty imposed on domestic importers as part of the tariff schedule. Justice Gorsuch’s stopping-point concern reinforces that, if “regulate” silently includes setting tariff rates, the foreign-property nexus and transaction architecture do little limiting work and IEEPA becomes an atextual substitute for Congress’s tariff-specific statutes. Even accounting for greater presidential flexibility in foreign affairs, separation-of-powers principles counsel that Congress must speak clearly before displacing the long-established trade-and-revenue framework, so we should decide on statutory grounds and not reach nondelegation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains that §1702(a)(1)(B) uses capacious verbs—especially “regulate” and “prohibit”—and expressly reaches “importation,” so a tariff could be recast as a form of import regulation during an emergency. But as Justice Kagan persuasively frames it, the key limiter is not an atextual magnitude carveout; it is the statute’s object: “transactions involving … property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” which naturally fits blocking and transactional controls rather than a generally applicable border exaction imposed on domestic importers as an incident of entry. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch reinforce why that matters structurally: accepting tariffs here would drain the foreign-property nexus of work and effectively turn IEEPA into a general tariff statute despite Congress’s detailed, tariff-specific delegations elsewhere. On that textual and structural mismatch, the President lacks statutory authorization, so we should resolve the case on statutory grounds without reaching nondelegation or other constitutional theories.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that IEEPA’s broad verbs like “regulate” and its reference to “importation” can naturally encompass tariffs—cannot be divorced from the limiting objects Congress chose: “transactions involving… property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest.” As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, that foreign-property/transaction architecture fits asset blocking and transactional prohibitions, not a generally applicable border exaction imposed on domestic importers that functions as trade-and-revenue policy. And as the Chief Justice stresses, accepting the Government’s reading would silently displace Congress’s detailed tariff statutes and, in structural terms, transfer core foreign-commerce and fiscal levers to the Executive without clear congressional direction—an expansion we should not infer by implication. Consistent with a merits-first approach, I would resolve this on straightforward statutory meaning rather than letting emergency framing or doctrinal shortcuts obscure whether Congress actually authorized tariffs here.

John Roberts.reasoning: The President’s authority must “stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself,” and here the Government principally invokes IEEPA as the statutory source. But imposing across-the-board tariffs is a decision of major economic and political consequence traditionally controlled by Congress through specific tariff statutes, and § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s transactional powers to “regulate,” “block,” or “prohibit” dealings in property do not clearly speak to a revenue-raising tariff regime that alters the tariff schedule. Under a major-questions/clear-statement approach, we should not read IEEPA’s general emergency language to silently displace Congress’s detailed trade and revenue framework; at a minimum, the absence of a clear delegation places the President in Youngstown’s zone where congressional authorization is lacking and the asserted power is at its “lowest ebb.” Foreign-affairs context may broaden permissible regulation of cross-border transactions, but it does not erase the requirement that Congress clearly authorize an instrument as consequential as tariffs where Congress has legislated specifically elsewhere.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The ordinary meaning and statutory context of § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorize the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified dealings in property and related transactions during an emergency; a tariff, by contrast, is a generally applicable import exaction that functions as a trade and revenue instrument rather than a transaction-specific restriction on “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest.” Reading IEEPA to permit tariffs would stretch a targeted emergency blocking statute into a broad tariff statute and risk making Congress’s more specific tariff-and-trade enactments superfluous, an interpretation statutory structure counsels against. Historical practice under TWEA-era cases like Yoshida cannot overcome IEEPA’s narrower post-1977 design—adopted against the backdrop of persistent, often nonmilitary emergencies—and courts should be especially reluctant to infer such a significant transfer of Congress’s foreign-commerce and taxing levers absent unmistakably clear text. Because the statute does not clearly confer tariff authority, I would resolve the case on statutory grounds and avoid the delegation question, consistent with separation-of-powers principles and judicial caution in foreign-affairs-adjacent disputes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the statute-first approach I have used in emergency-powers cases, the question is whether the President’s asserted tariff power fits within IEEPA’s specific predicates and operative authorizations. Section 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate… transactions” in “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” which historically has functioned as a transactions-and-asset-blocking power; a generally applicable tariff is instead a revenue-raising and trade-regulating instrument that Congress has conferred through distinct, carefully conditioned tariff statutes, not through IEEPA’s emergency blocking framework. Reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would collapse the statutory architecture Congress built across IEEPA, the NEA, and the trade laws by converting a targeted emergency tool into a broad, procedurally unconstrained tariff authority—an interpretation especially disfavored given the absence of clear textual indicia that Congress meant to delegate so significant a power. Because the best reading of IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, the Court need not reach the government’s fallback unconstitutional-delegation contention.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Starting with text and structure, IEEPA § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, direct and compel, nullify, void, prevent or prohibit” transactions in “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest,” a targeted transaction-/property-blocking power that does not clearly encompass imposing across-the-board tariffs—an archetypal revenue-and-trade instrument Congress has historically delegated, when at all, through specific tariff statutes. Reading “regulate … importation” to include tariff exactions would convert a limited emergency sanctions tool into a sweeping trade-and-tax authority without the clear statement one would expect where Congress transfers so weighty a power, and it would also strain the statute’s foreign-property nexus where tariffs are assessed against domestic importers after entry. Because this case can and should be resolved on statutory grounds, I would not reach the government’s fallback nondelegation argument; but the breadth of the government’s reading underscores why courts must enforce IEEPA’s textual limits rather than allow emergency powers to expand by implication. Finally, the Government’s suggestion of nonreviewability cannot displace the judiciary’s role in saying what the statute authorizes, especially where the Executive’s fast-moving use of emergency authority threatens to evade ordinary legal constraints and meaningful judicial review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA’s trigger conditions may well be satisfied once a national emergency is declared and the President identifies an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” but the operative delegation still has to do the work Congress wrote: §1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate,” “direct and compel,” or “prohibit” transactions involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest.” A tariff is not naturally a regulation of a specified foreign-owned property interest or a prohibition on a described transaction; it is a generally applicable import exaction imposed on domestic importers, functioning as revenue-raising and trade policy—an authority Congress has historically conferred through distinct, tariff-specific statutes rather than through IEEPA’s transaction- and property-centered verbs and objects. Reading IEEPA to allow across-the-board tariffs would thus expand a targeted emergency tool into a general trade-and-tax instrument without a textual hook, and that limit comes from the statute’s object (“property” with a foreign interest) and structure—not from judicial skepticism about the policy’s size or novelty. Because the best reading of the text does not authorize tariffs, the Court need not—and should not—reach the government’s fallback unconstitutional-delegation question.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the text. Section 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified dealings in “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest”; its most natural linguistic interpretation targets transaction- and property-based controls (blocking, freezing, directing transfers), not the imposition of generally applicable import tariffs that operate as a revenue-raising incident of entry. Reading “regulate” to include tariffing risks making IEEPA’s carefully cabined, property-with-a-foreign-interest limitation and its transaction-focused verbs do little work—effectively converting an emergency economic-control statute into a roving trade-and-tax power Congress has traditionally conferred with far more specificity. The government’s “tariffs-as-regulation” theory also lacks any principled, administrable stopping point in the statute: once “regulate” includes setting tariff rates, nothing in § 1702 supplies a textual standard to distinguish permissible “emergency” tariffs from ordinary trade policy, inviting exactly the sort of atextual policymaking courts are not free to supply. And separation-of-powers concerns reinforce adhering to the statute’s limits rather than enlarging them to spare executive inconvenience; Congress may authorize tariffs in emergencies, but it must do so clearly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Imposing across-the-board tariffs is a major policy decision with enormous domestic economic and revenue consequences, and Congress does not ordinarily "hide elephants in mouseholes"—especially where it has enacted detailed, tariff-specific statutes when it wants to confer that power. IEEPA’s text and structure focus on blocking or regulating specific transactions in property in which a foreign country or national has an interest; reading § 1702(a)(1)(B) to authorize tariffs would convert a targeted emergency tool into a general trade-and-tax authority that Congress has historically reserved to itself. Although the major-questions canon "does not translate" in the same way in foreign-affairs and national-security contexts, the asserted power here functions as domestic economic regulation and taxation, placing the President at least in a Youngstown category 2.5 posture absent clear congressional authorization. Because the best reading of IEEPA does not clearly authorize tariffs, I would resolve the case on statutory grounds and avoid the nondelegation question.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with the text: § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified categories of foreign-connected transactions and dealings in “property” or “interests in property,” which fits asset-blocking and transactional restrictions—not the imposition of a generally applicable tariff (a revenue-raising border exaction that operates by changing the legal duty owed on importation). Read in statutory structure and historical context, Congress has typically conferred tariff authority through specific trade statutes with rate schedules, procedural constraints, and delegation limits; converting IEEPA’s emergency transaction powers into a broad tariff power is an unusually expansive reading that a reasonable reader would not attribute to Congress without clearer direction, especially given the major economic and political significance of tariff policy. Because the best reading of IEEPA does not reach tariffs, I would not proceed to the government’s fallback constitutional-delegation question. Dames & Moore and related cases recognizing robust emergency authority over foreign assets do not supply the missing statutory hook here, because they involved regulation and disposition of property and claims—not the creation of a new tariff regime.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: IEEPA’s text in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified foreign-linked “transactions” and dealings in “property” subject to U.S. jurisdiction; that kind of targeted transaction-blocking authority is not a clear statutory grant to impose across-the-board tariffs, a distinct Congress-controlled trade-and-revenue instrument that Congress has historically conferred through specific tariff statutes. Treating an emergency statute aimed at freezing or blocking particular economic dealings as a general tariff power would functionally expand executive power at Congress’s expense without the requisite clear statement—precisely the sort of implied “core” Article II argument resting on indefinite constitutional grounding that I have been skeptical of. The Court should resolve this merits question rather than allow jurisdictional channeling or nonjusticiability theories to delay review where the legality turns on straightforward statutory meaning. Because the better reading is that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, the Court need not reach the government’s fallback unconstitutional-delegation question.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes the President to impose tariffs under 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) during a declared national emergency.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (IEEPA); related separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns appear in the consolidated briefing posture.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (importers challenging the tariff) argue that IEEPA’s text does not confer tariff-setting power, which is traditionally and constitutionally legislative and has been addressed by Congress through distinct, tariff-specific statutes. They contend § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes targeted controls over transactions/property interests (e.g., blocking, regulating transfers) rather than imposing across-the-board import duties, and that reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would improperly expand emergency power and bypass Congress’s detailed tariff framework. They also press that the Supreme Court should resolve the question promptly to provide nationwide certainty and finality, and they resist efforts to sidestep merits review through forum/jurisdictional maneuvering (e.g., transfer to the Court of International Trade) where the dispute turns on IEEPA’s meaning rather than the tariff schedule.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the federal government/President) maintain that IEEPA’s broad grant to 'regulate' or 'prohibit' certain economic transactions involving foreign interests can encompass the imposition of tariffs as a tool to address an 'unusual and extraordinary threat' declared under the statute. They also suggest that challenges to the President’s emergency determinations and compliance involve nonjusticiable political questions or are committed to congressional oversight mechanisms rather than judicial second-guessing. In addition, the government has argued (at least in the lower-court posture reflected in the excerpts) that the case belongs in the specialized trade forum (the Court of International Trade) and can be transferred without reaching the merits, implying the district court should avoid deciding the substantive IEEPA question in the first instance.
key_precedents: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc.
BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point: §1702(a)(1)(B) uses broad verbs and Congress borrowed TWEA language against the backdrop of Yoshida, so a border charge might be viewed as one way to “regulate” importation. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize, tariffs are a distinct, historically tariff-specific instrument of enormous economic and political significance, and Congress has repeatedly legislated in that space with tailored triggers and limits—making it implausible that IEEPA silently confers an effectively open-ended duty-setting power. Under Youngstown, the question is not whether tariffs might be useful in an emergency but whether enacted law clearly authorizes them; IEEPA’s transaction-and-property framework (blocking, licensing, prohibiting dealings) does not clearly extend to generally applicable, revenue-raising duties. A narrow holding—IEEPA permits embargoes, licensing, and targeted import prohibitions tied to foreign interests, but not general tariffs—answers the statutory question without reaching broader constitutional issues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the TWEA/Yoshida lineage and the breadth of §1702(a)(1)(B)’s verbs, but that is not enough to turn IEEPA into a tariff statute. As the Chief Justice explains, IEEPA’s text and structure are organized around controlling transactions and foreign property interests (blocking, prohibiting, licensing), and reading “regulate … importation” to include generally applicable duties would effectively sideline Congress’s tariff-specific frameworks—an implausible construction that makes large portions of that scheme functionally meaningless. Justice Kagan is right that the emergency predicates narrow the statute somewhat, but they do not supply the missing delegation to impose “duties,” and we should not treat congressional “awareness” of a lower-court gloss as a roving incorporation that displaces the enacted text. Under Youngstown’s source-of-authority principle, the President must point to valid statutory or constitutional authority, and neither IEEPA’s words nor Article II’s residual foreign-affairs power clearly confers the asserted tariff power here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the TWEA/Yoshida lineage—Congress borrowed similar language and may have legislated with that gloss in mind. But that inference cannot do the work of text and structure: as the Chief Justice notes, IEEPA is built around transactional and property-interest controls (blocking, prohibiting, licensing), and reading §1702(a)(1)(B) to authorize generally applicable, revenue-like import duties would effectively “upend” Congress’s tariff-specific architecture in Title 19 without a clear statement. Even if a surcharge might be one way to “regulate” importation in the abstract, IEEPA’s context and Congress’s repeated practice of conferring tariff authority through tailored delegations make it implausible that Congress silently transferred such a central Article I tool by general emergency verbs. I would therefore hold, on the merits first, that IEEPA does not confer an across-the-board tariff power of the kind asserted here, leaving constitutional questions (including nondelegation) unnecessary to decide.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Congress borrowed TWEA language after Yoshida and that §1702(a)(1)(B)’s broad verbs (“regulate” and “prohibit”) reach “importation,” making a border charge a conceivable regulatory tool in an emergency. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, IEEPA’s text and structure are aimed at controlling transactions and property interests—blocking, freezing, licensing, and prohibiting dealings—not at imposing generally applicable duties that would sidestep Congress’s detailed Title 19 tariff schemes. The Yoshida gloss cannot do the work of a clear statutory fit where the asserted power would effectively relocate a quintessential Article I foreign-commerce/tax choice to the President by implication and in a novel way that risks turning an emergency sanctions statute into a roving trade code. Under Youngstown’s source-of-authority principle, I do not see IEEPA as clearly authorizing tariffs of general applicability, even if it authorizes embargoes and targeted import prohibitions tied to foreign property interests.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s point—that Congress has enacted tariff-specific frameworks and that this use of IEEPA is economically momentous—has force, but it rests on importing a clear-statement threshold not found in IEEPA’s own design. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Congress built meaningful predicates into IEEPA (an "unusual and extraordinary threat," a declared emergency, and action taken to address that emergency), and once those triggers are satisfied, the operative authorization to "regulate" and "prohibit" the "importation" of covered property is textually capacious enough to include a border charge as a regulatory tool rather than a freestanding revenue measure. Justice Barrett’s contextual reading (that IEEPA is mainly about blocking/licensing foreign property interests) is plausible, but the statute expressly reaches importation itself, and I do not think we should move the ‘goalposts’ by requiring tariff-specific “magic words” where Congress instead chose comprehensive transactional language with built-in limiting standards. Nor do I see a nondelegation backstop here, because the emergency trigger and nexus/fit constraint supply the kind of intelligible principle our cases have long accepted.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the TWEA/Yoshida lineage—Congress borrowed similar words and may have known a surcharge had been sustained—but that inference cannot displace IEEPA’s most natural linguistic reading and statutory context. Section 1702(a)(1)(B) speaks in the idiom of sanctions: regulating or prohibiting discrete transactions in property with a foreign “interest,” tools like blocking, licensing, and embargoes, not imposing generally applicable “duties” that function as a revenue-raising tariff schedule. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, accepting the government’s reading would make Congress’s tariff-specific delegations and their careful limits largely surplusage, effectively converting an emergency transactions statute into a roving tariff code. Separation-of-powers baselines counsel that such a major shift in Article I foreign-commerce and taxing authority requires a clear statement, and IEEPA does not supply it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that tariffs are a familiar Article I instrument and that Congress has enacted tariff-specific schemes elsewhere, so using IEEPA here looks novel and economically significant. But I do not think the major-questions/clear-statement rule translates in the same way in the foreign-affairs emergency context, where Congress has long used broad delegations against the backdrop of some independent Article II authority, and IEEPA itself contains meaningful predicates (an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” a declared emergency, and a foreign nexus). On the statutory text, §1702(a)(1)(B)’s authorization to “regulate…importation” of property in which a foreign country or national has an interest, coupled with IEEPA’s TWEA lineage and the Yoshida gloss, makes it at least a permissible reading that an import surcharge can be one tool to regulate importation in an emergency. I agree with the Chief Justice that we should avoid turning IEEPA into a “roving tariff code,” but that concern is better handled through limiting principles tied to the statute’s foreign-property-interest nexus and emergency-purpose requirements rather than by imposing a categorical tariff carveout not found in the text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the TWEA/Yoshida lineage: that Congress borrowed materially similar language and may have understood it to reach an import surcharge. But even accepting that history, the ordinary meaning and statutory context of §1702(a)(1)(B)—embedded in a regime of blocking, licensing, and prohibiting dealings in foreign property interests—fit transaction controls and embargoes far more naturally than a generally applicable duty, especially given Congress’s repeated use of tariff-specific statutes with tailored triggers and constraints, as the Chief emphasizes. Justice Kagan is right that IEEPA has demanding predicates, but those predicates do not answer the antecedent question whether Congress actually authorized this distinct instrument; reading “regulate … importation” to include an open-ended tariff power would press IEEPA “for all it is worth” on a question of vast economic and political significance without a clear textual fit. On the merits-first statutory reading, we can hold IEEPA permits prohibitions and licensing tied to foreign interests, but not the imposition of generally applicable duties absent clearer authorization—thereby also avoiding the serious structural concern of relocating a quintessential Article I fiscal choice by implication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Congress borrowed TWEA language against the backdrop of Yoshida and that §1702(a)(1)(B) uses broad verbs (“regulate”/“prohibit”) reaching “importation.” But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, breadth in an emergency sanctions statute is not the same thing as a clear delegation to impose generally applicable duties—an instrument Congress has addressed through tariff-specific statutes with tailored predicates and constraints. I do not think legislative “awareness” of a lower-court construction can do the separation-of-powers work here: absent a clear textual signal authorizing duties, we should not read §1702(a)(1)(B) to relocate core tariff-setting choices from Congress to the Executive by implication. Accepting the Government’s theory risks converting IEEPA from a transactions-and-property control statute into a roving trade/revenue tool, with significant structural ripple effects that our interpretive rules should avoid.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Youngstown, the President must point to authority that “stem[s] either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself,” and here the only claimed source is IEEPA § 1702(a)(1)(B). That provision’s terms—authorizing the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign property interests—do not clearly speak to imposing generally applicable import duties, a power Congress has addressed through tariff-specific statutes and historically exercised as a core legislative function. Given the novelty and breadth of using IEEPA to set tariffs—an action of substantial economic and political significance—the major-questions/clear-delegation principle counsels that Congress must speak clearly before we read emergency economic authorities to upend the established tariff framework. Reading § 1702(a)(1)(B) to authorize tariffs would risk converting a targeted sanctions statute into effectively open-ended revenue and trade-regulation power, a result inconsistent with statutory text and past practice.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Reading § 1702(a)(1)(B) in its immediate statutory context, IEEPA authorizes the President to regulate or prohibit specified transactions and property interests involving foreign parties (e.g., blocking or controlling dealings), not to impose revenue-raising import duties; treating “regulate … importation” as a tariff power would make Congress’s separate, tariff-specific delegations largely meaningless and distort IEEPA’s sanctions-focused structure. Because tariffs are a traditional legislative instrument and Congress has provided detailed mechanisms for them elsewhere, I will not infer so consequential a delegation from IEEPA’s general terms absent a clear statement. This case does not ask the Court to defer to “concededly unlawful” executive action or to treat the statutory question as nonjusticiable; rather, it requires enforcing the limits Congress actually enacted, even in an emergency. Whatever the President’s residual Article II authority in foreign affairs, he may not unilaterally supply statutory power Congress did not confer for tariffs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Reading IEEPA in its full statutory and historical setting, Congress has repeatedly addressed tariffs through distinct, tariff-specific delegations (e.g., §§ 232 and 301) that contain tailored triggers, procedures, and limits, which strongly suggests that an across-the-board import duty is not silently embedded in IEEPA’s emergency power to “regulate” transactions involving foreign interests. Section 1702(a)(1)(B) is best understood—consistent with IEEPA’s TWEA lineage and this Court’s cases—as authorizing controls on property and transactional incidents (blocking, freezing, prohibiting transfers), not the imposition of a revenue-raising exaction that sits at the core of Congress’s power of the purse. Proceeding merits-first, the Court should decide the scope of the statutory grant before entertaining forum or remedial maneuvering, and a sweeping tariff power in IEEPA would disrupt the broader architecture Congress enacted for trade and emergencies and raise serious separation-of-powers concerns that Congress did not clearly accept. Because the claimed authority lacks the kind of express, tariff-focused delegation that has historically accompanied presidential tariff actions, I would hold IEEPA does not authorize these tariffs.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: IEEPA must be read in light of its text, structure, and the historical triggers Congress attached to extraordinary economic powers, and the President’s peacetime imposition of generally applicable tariffs is a novel fit with § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s transaction-and-property focused tools. Although IEEPA borrows language from TWEA, Congress’s post-TWEA enactments built detailed, tariff-specific frameworks, signaling that import duties remain a quintessential Article I foreign-commerce/tax choice that requires a clearer statutory authorization than a general emergency "regulate" clause. Historical practice under TWEA involved blocking, licensing, and targeted import controls tied to wartime or closely analogous emergencies, not a wholesale displacement of Congress’s tariff scheme whenever an emergency is declared. Accepting the Government’s reading would expand exceptional emergency authority beyond its historically accepted bounds and allow the Executive to bypass Congress where Congress has legislated with specificity, so I would hold IEEPA does not authorize these tariffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA contains meaningful triggering conditions: the President must declare a national emergency to meet an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” and §1702 then authorizes specified actions only as necessary to address that emergency. Once those predicates are satisfied, the operative verbs—authorizing the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” transactions involving property in which a foreign country or national has an interest—are written in broad, ordinary terms that can encompass regulating importation by imposing a monetary exaction at the border as one means of controlling those foreign-involved transactions. Petitioners’ point that Congress has also enacted tariff-specific statutes goes to policy and legislative design, not atextual limits: Congress did not carve “tariffs” out of IEEPA’s capacious delegation, and courts should not move the goalposts by demanding “magic words” like “duties” when the statute’s standards and emergency predicates already constrain the discretion. On nondelegation, IEEPA supplies an intelligible principle—an emergency tied to an extraordinary foreign threat and action calibrated to address it—so this is not “virtually unfettered” authority of the Schechter sort.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The most natural reading of § 1702(a)(1)(B)—authorizing the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified transactions involving “property in which any foreign country or a national thereof has any interest”—targets control of discrete dealings with foreign property interests (blocking, freezing, conditioning transfers), not the imposition of revenue-raising import duties of general applicability. Reading “regulate … importation” to include tariffs would risk making Congress’s detailed, tariff-specific statutes largely surplusage, allowing the Executive to bypass the bounded rate-setting schemes and procedural constraints Congress elsewhere chose to enact. Separation-of-powers baselines reinforce that conclusion: absent a clear statement that Congress meant to hand the President a tariff power of such breadth under an emergency statute, courts should not presume it—especially where the asserted authority approaches a delegation with distinctive nondelegation sensitivities. Dames & Moore confirms IEEPA’s lineage and validates certain emergency controls over foreign assets, but it does not supply a warrant to treat IEEPA as a roving tariff statute that displaces Congress’s carefully calibrated trade laws.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: In the foreign-affairs/national-security context that IEEPA addresses, the major-questions clear-statement canon generally does not operate the same way it does in domestic regulatory cases, because Congress often legislates through broad emergency delegations against the backdrop of the President’s independent Article II responsibilities (Youngstown category 2.5). On the best reading of § 1702(a)(1)(B) in context, Congress borrowed operative language from TWEA after Yoshida had construed that language to permit an import-duty surcharge, and Congress’s enactment history (including the House Report) indicates awareness and acceptance of that understanding. Applying the traditional intelligible-principle framework, IEEPA supplies the general policy and limiting standards—an “unusual and extraordinary threat,” a declared national emergency, and regulation of specified foreign-related transactions/property interests—while leaving the President to choose among tools, including tariffs, to address the emergency. Because Congress knows how to impose narrower, tariff-specific limits when it wants to, and did not do so here, I would uphold the President’s authority under IEEPA to impose the challenged tariffs during the declared emergency.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Start with ordinary meaning and statutory context: § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified transactions and dealings in “property” in which a foreign country or national has an interest—language drawn from TWEA and historically used for blocking/freezing and transactional controls, not for levying revenue-raising import duties. Reading that provision to smuggle in a generally applicable tariff power would disregard the distinct statutory framework in Title 19 where Congress delegates tariff authority expressly, and it would press IEEPA “for all it is worth” to accomplish an action of vast economic and political significance—an interpretive context that counsels against such an expansive construction absent clear textual fit. Only after that merits reading do the structural concerns come into view: because the Constitution separately assigns the power to lay “Duties” to Congress, construing IEEPA to authorize tariff-setting would raise serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation questions by transferring a quintessentially legislative taxing choice through general emergency language. The better reading is that IEEPA permits targeted regulation or prohibition of imports as transactions (e.g., embargoes or licensing), but not the imposition of tariffs as duties.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: IEEPA’s baseline rule is that the President may “regulate” or “prohibit” specified categories of transactions and property interests involving foreign interests during an emergency, and nothing in § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s text clearly displaces Congress’s longstanding, detailed control over tariff-setting as a revenue-raising and trade-calibrating instrument. Reading IEEPA to authorize across-the-board tariffs would effect a major reallocation of power—allowing the Executive to bypass Congress’s tariff-specific statutes and frameworks—without a clear textual statement that Congress meant to confer that extraordinary authority. The government’s reliance on broad, indeterminate notions of emergency “core” executive power cannot supply what the statute does not clearly grant; in our system, enacted law binds executive officers, and courts should not adopt interpretations that indirectly expand executive power by insulating tariff policy from congressional constraint. Given the institutional consequences and the absence of a clear statutory signal that “regulate … importation” includes imposing general duties, I would hold that IEEPA does not authorize these tariffs.
